finding.title: Buffer Overflow
finding.trigger: Sending a packet larger than sizeof(uint32_t) from the client
finding.assumptions: The recvfrom function does not check the size of the incoming packet, and the buffer is not dynamically sized.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the recvfrom usage: the buffer pointer is &number and the length argument is sizeof(uint32_t), so the kernel will copy at most 4 bytes into the 4‑byte buffer. For a UDP datagram socket, if the incoming packet exceeds the supplied buffer size, the excess data is discarded (truncated) rather than written beyond the buffer. No unchecked memory access occurs. No other code paths or size checks are needed because the length parameter already enforces the limit.

finding.title: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
finding.trigger: Inputting a value that exceeds the range of uint32_t
finding.assumptions: The input is not validated to ensure it fits within the range of uint32_t.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the source is a scanf with %x storing into a uint32_t variable (line 49). In standard C, the %x conversion writes into an unsigned int; on common 64‑bit platforms unsigned int is 32‑bits, matching uint32_t, so the conversion cannot overflow. If the input value is larger than can be represented, the conversion fails and no value is stored, preventing wrap‑around. The subsequent call to htonl (line 54) simply performs a byte‑swap on a 32‑bit value and does not perform arithmetic that could overflow. No other arithmetic operations use the value, so there is no path from the untrusted input to an integer overflow operation. Therefore the reported CWE‑391 claim is unfounded.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Inputting a value that could be interpreted as a command by the shell
finding.assumptions: The input is not properly sanitized before being used in a system call.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Reviewed lines 48‑50: they contain only a prompt and an error message. The printf on line 48 uses a string literal format specifier and prints the integer read by scanf; it does not pass user input as a format string or command. No system or exec calls are present in the fragment. Thus there is no path from untrusted input to an OS command execution.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: Inputting a value that could be interpreted as a command by the shell
finding.assumptions: The input is not properly sanitized before being used in a system call.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the user input is parsed with scanf("%x", &number), which stores a 32‑bit unsigned integer into the variable 'number'. The subsequent printf calls are only printing string literals: line 48 prints the prompt "Server (You): ", and line 50 prints the Korean string "숫자를 입력하세요.". None of these printf calls include user data or invoke a shell command. The code never passes the user input to system(), exec*(), popen(), or any other OS command invocation. Thus there is no path from the untrusted source to a dangerous OS command execution. The sink identified in the report is incorrectly marked.
